- **Cause:** the knot was lofted from uniform rounded sections; nothing shaped the face a four-in-hand shows.
- **Fix:** the knot's front face carries the band the last pass wraps across the front (Ro Li of Li Ro Li Co T, Fink and
  Mao 1999), 1.8 mm proud above a lower edge sloping across the knot, and a 2.5 mm dimple under it where the blade
  drops through (`TIE.band`, `edge`, `slope`, `dimple` in fit.ts, estimates read from the LOC photographs);
  17 rows up the knot in place of 8. After it: 4.9 mm and 2.7 mm.
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/fit.test.js "the four-in-hand shows its wrapped band and a dimple under it".

### Fixed 2026-11-18: dressed Wilbur's coat swelled into a barrel with the arms down, shirt showed at the shoulder seam, the hat read as a top hat (KB-HUMANS-WILBURSUIT3, humans)

- **Repro:** `dressPerson(engine, wilbur, 'townsman-1910')` on the Wilbur Character Creator rig (asset library, not in
  git), idle clip, arms down (dressed6): the coat stood 5 to 8 cm off his sides from the chest to the hem and 1.8 cm
  further out at the back than the plumb line, a white sliver showed at the shoulder seam, and the hat had a straight
  11 cm crown with a flat top. Measured with the arms lowered 58 degrees: coat half breadth 0.222 m against a chest of
  0.169 m; back -0.175 m against shoulder blades at -0.137 m.
- **Cause:** (1) the rig stands in an A-pose; its armpit and the roots of the lats and deltoids stand out under the arm
  and carry part of the arm's weight, so the trunk's ring at the chest was 3 cm wider each side than once the arms come
  down, and the sack hang carried that width plumb to the hem; the shirt and vest under it each clear the body's rings
  up to 3 cm above and below, so rows below the armpit carried it too. (2) The coat flutes only stood out, never in, so
  they moved the whole back out by their height. (3) Every sleeve started at the same place along the arm, so the
  shirt sleeve's raw top edge stood level with the coat's, above the coat's yoke over the shoulder point. (4) The hat
  had no rounded crown.
- **Fix:** the fit also measures the trunk with the arms hanging (each vertex moved by its arm's share of the turn that
  brings the upper arm straight down, as linear blend skinning poses it); the hang takes each row's ring in by the most
  the trunk's ring comes in within the layers' floor reach, and each row still clears its own ring at rest. Flutes are
  crests and troughs about the plumb line, a trough never deeper than the row's room. Each sleeve starts a ring
  (`SLEEVE_LAP`, 12 mm) further in than the sleeve beneath. `GarmentSpec.dome` rounds a hat's crown over; the
  townsman wears a 5 1/4 inch derby on a 2 inch brim (period catalogues as summarised by Vintage Dancer; LOC
  photographs). On Wilbur with the arms lowered the coat's half breadth is now 0.187 to 0.204 m (the widest over the
  seat) and its back -0.157 to -0.166 m; shirt seen through the coat over the shoulders: 22 vertices before, 10 after
  (all under the left armpit's back, open).
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/fit.test.js "the townsman coat hangs from the chest as worn with the arms down"
  (a lean test body with arm roots; old: the coat 30.5 to 50 mm off the lowered chest between waist and hip, bound the
  layers plus 4 mm), "the coat sleeve covers the shirt sleeve at the shoulder seam" (old: 18 to 50 shirt vertices
  uncovered) and "the townsman wears a derby" (old: an 11 cm straight crown).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: dressed Wilbur showed a white bib at the neck: no tie, a closed tube of a collar, flat lapels; folded V rows parted when posed (KB-HUMANS-NECKCHEST1, humans)

- **Repro:** `dressPerson(engine, wilbur, 'townsman-1910')` rendered at a medium shot (dressed5 in the asset library, not in
  git): a flat white V from the neck to the vest, the shirt collar a closed 2 1/4 inch tube, no tie, and the coat lapels
  0.4 mm over the coat (no roll, no notch), next to the Library of Congress photographs of the Wright brothers (1903 to
  1910: a high collar, a dark tie, rolled lapels). Adding a tie then measured it 20 mm through the coat in the test
  body's turn and lean (`fitPenetration`), where there was no crossing.
- **Cause:** the outfit had no tie garment and the fit no tie or collar points; the lapel strip was laid flat on the cloth.
  The 20 mm was a fit bug: a V neckline folds a column's rows above its cut onto one point, but the yoke rows read their
  skin weights at their anchors and the collar rows above read the lattice, so the folded points parted (0.12 mm on the
  test body's coat in a turn and lean) into slivers whose normals point anywhere, which the measure read as 20 mm.
- **Fix:** `GarmentCut` `'tie'` (`knot`: four-in-hand or bow) and `GarmentSpec.points` (wing points); the lapels roll
  (`LAPEL` in fit.ts) with a folded edge, an outer edge and a gorge line falling to the point, the coat collar a ring
  step short of it; what lies on cloth (lapels, the tie's blade) takes the weights of the cloth under it; folded rows
  read their weights the way the row under the cut does. Sources: Gordon 1895, Croonborg 1907, Fink and Mao 1999, LOC
  ppprs.00683. The roll, point and tie widths are estimates (fit.ts LAPEL, POINTS, TIE).
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/fit.test.js "the townsman wears a four-in-hand", "the shirt's wing collar parts at
  the front", "the coat lapels roll" (old: no tie; collar front 57 mm up; lapel 2 mm off the coat) and "the rows folded
  onto a V neckline cut stay one point when the body moves" (old: parted by 0.12 mm).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: dressed Wilbur's coat still bellied out round the front waist and came back in below it (KB-HUMANS-WILBURSUIT2, humans)

- **Repro:** `fitOutfit` of `townsman-1910` on the Wilbur Character Creator rig (asset library, not in git), rendered
  at a medium shot (dressed3): a round belly at the front waist, the coat's front corners and sides standing out over
  the waist and coming back in below it. Sliced through the coat: 14 cm either side of the centre the front came back
  in 8.0 mm below 1.1 m, the half breadth 6.7 mm; outer normals there pointed 0.13 down (the shadow under the belly).
- **Cause:** the sack hang and the plumb (KB-HUMANS-WILBURSUIT1) moved each ring radius by its centre's shift along its
  own angle only, which slides every point sideways by the rest of the shift. Wilbur's trunk centre line runs 2.8 cm
  back from the belly (1.10 m) to 1.00 m, so the rings below were turned against the ones above, and narrower at the
  front corners. The centre line alone checked plumb, which hid it.
- **Fix:** each ring is re-centred exactly (`recentre` in fit.ts: the ring's reach at every angle seen from the new
  centre, the radius run linearly with the angle between points, so an unmoved ring comes back unchanged); the hang's
  envelope and the plumb both run on one straight centre line and each ring goes back to its own centre once. After it,
  on Wilbur, the front comes back in under 0.6 mm anywhere 14 cm either side of the centre. The coat folds added in the
  same work keep this: their height no longer follows the spare girth row by row (which shrank over the seat and pulled
  the back in 2 mm), and they are symmetric with the deepest over the back seam.
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/fit.test.js "the townsman coat hangs plumb all round the front over a belly" (a
  lean test body with a 4 cm belly and the seat as far back; old: the front 8 cm out came back in 4.0 mm) and "the
  townsman coat hangs plumb from the chest on a lean body" (with the folds: back 2 mm in at 0.9 m before the fold fix).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: dressPerson put the outfit in the active scene, then parented it under a model in another scene; humans had no owner/lifetime fixture (KB-HUMANS-OWNERS1, humans)

- **Repro:** a model loaded into a scene that is not the active one (`engine.createScene`), `addPerson` on it, then
  `dressPerson(engine, person, 'townsman-1910')`: "Foreign parent". A first owner/lifetime fixture for humans read 0 of
  26 cases passing, under both `addPerson` and `dressPerson`.
- **Cause:** `dressPerson` parsed the outfit with `parseGLTFAsync(engine, ...)`, which registers the model in the scene
  active when the call starts (the default scene), and then set the outfit's root under the person's model, which lived
  in its own scene. The other 0-of-26 failures were the first fixture's, not the package's: it did not list the
  caller's model (itself a scene registration) and the person's materials plugin among its dependencies, it parsed the
  model with the async loader (whose work after its first await counts as the owner under test, so the model's draws
  and buffers read as the person's), and it did not warm materials' skin profile table, one 64x64 texture made once
  per device on the first skin and kept for the device's life (as `oit` warms materials' default textures).
- **Fix:** `dressPerson` loads the outfit inside a scope over the model's scene (`sceneScope` from
  `packages/shared/scene-scope.js`), so the outfit, its cloth materials and its Animation all join the model's scene
  whatever scene is active. The fixture `packages/humans/test/owner-lifetime.fixture.js` parses the model
  synchronously, lists it (and, for the outfit, the person's materials, Animation and Animator) as dependencies, makes
  the outfit's person without hands so that dependency finishes inside its own scope, and warms the skin table.
  `npm run check:owners -- --packages=humans`: 26 of 26 on the CPU, on WebGPU and on the WebGL2 compatibility layer.
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/lifetime.test.js "dressPerson puts the outfit in the scene of a model that is
  not in the active scene, and takes it off again" (old: Foreign parent), and the owner/lifetime fixture.

### Fixed 2026-11-18: dressed Wilbur showed a wedge of skin at both sleeve tops and a coat that bellied at the waist (KB-HUMANS-WILBURSUIT1, humans)

- **Repro:** `fitOutfit` of `townsman-1910` on the Wilbur Character Creator rig (the asset library's
  `people/kitty-hawk-1903/wilbur`, not in git), rendered in the idle clip with the arms down: an orange wedge showed at
  the top outside of each sleeve, and the coat swelled over the waist and came in to a hem 2.3 cm narrower than its
  chest (front 1.5 cm and back 1.1 cm in again below the belly). At rest `fitPenetration` read 0. The test body
  reproduces both once posed and once lean: lowered 80 degrees from its T-pose 14 upward shoulder vertices were bare,
  and `riggedTestBody(pose, { lean: true })` (chest broader than hips, the torso's centre forward at the belly and back
  at the waist) narrowed the coat 2.9 mm under its chest and brought its back in 5.8 mm.
- **Cause:** two. (1) Every garment vertex read its weights from its part's lattice by its height and angle round the
  trunk, and the trunk's slices hold no deltoid (its points weigh to the upper arm), so the yoke over the shoulder point
  took the chest's weights and stayed while the shoulder's cap turned down with the arm. (2) The sack drape's envelope,
  and the layer floor under every garment, compared ring radii taken round centres that sit up to 2.6 cm apart (the
  trunk's centre line on a real torso), so a ring centred forward read as wider: the coat bellied where the centre
  sat forward, and the hem came in where a lean man's hips are narrower than his chest.
- **Fix:** the rows over the shoulders take their weights from the body at their anchors (the body point under each,
  shared by every layer); floor and envelope move each ring's radii to one centre first; below the chest the sack coat
  hangs plumb (no column comes back in toward the hem, Gordon 1895); the cloth around the legs reads the cloth already on
  each leg at that height instead of the most it stands off anywhere above the knee. Measuring the fix showed a bug in
  the measure itself: `fitPenetration` took triangles with no area (a V neckline's folded rows) as surfaces, so the rest
  pose skinned by identity matrices read a 46 mm crossing where at rest it read none; such triangles are now left out.
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/fit.test.js "the coat over the shoulder points moves with the arm" (old: 14
  bare vertices at 80 degrees, 4 at 45), "the townsman coat hangs plumb from the chest on a lean body" (old: half
  breadth 0.198 at 1.10 m against the chest's 0.199) and "the rest pose skinned reads the same as no pose".

### Fixed 2026-11-18: the cast kit's cloth fit gave no sheen to seven of its eight fabrics (KB-HUMANS-SHEENZERO1, humans)

- **Repro:** `periodLobes(kind, [g, g, g])` from `@margoengine/humans/cast` for g 0.03, 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6: every kind but
  `cotton-corduroy` (denim, duck, shirting, worsted, flannel, polyester blend, silk) returns `sheenColor` [0, 0, 0],
  with `roughness` 0.5 or 0.6 (silk 0.5 to 0.9), so wool and cotton render as a matte GGX with no grazing rim.
- **Cause:** `fitLobes` in `packages/humans/src/cast.ts` fits the sheen as a least-squares weight over the measured
  samples after a GGX lobe at a fixed F0 of 0.04. With the roughness held at 0.5 or more that GGX lobe already
  overshoots the measured grazing reflectance, so the sheen weight that best fits the remainder is negative and is
  clamped to 0. The specular and the sheen need fitting together (or the F0 freed) rather than one after the other.
  Found while finding why the suits rendered flat black (a separate cause, the base colour, fixed with the garment fit
  of 2026-11-18); the dark worsted suit now reads as cloth without the sheen, but has no grazing rim.
  Freeing the specular (a KHR_materials_specular factor fitted with the sheen) still gives sheen 0: the model's target
  samples have no grazing rim for a sheen lobe to fit, so a wool fabric needs a fibre or fuzz sheen basis of its own
  (Zeltner, Burley and Chiang 2022, "Practical Multiple-Scattering Sheen Using Linearly Transformed Cosines";
  Estevez and Kulla 2017, "Production Friendly Microfacet Sheen BRDF"; Irawan and Marschner 2012, "Specular
  reflection from woven cloth").
- **Fix:** the measured model gains a layer of loose fibre ends over the weave (`FabricOptics.fuzz`): single scattering
  in a thin slab of fibre microflakes (Jakob et al. 2010) whose normals spread as sin^4 from the cloth normal (the fibre
  distribution of the Charlie sheen, Estevez and Kulla 2017; the volumetric fibre layer of Zeltner, Burley and Chiang
  2022), each flake reflecting white by Fresnel and passing the rest into the dyed fibre, the weave seen through it.
  Depths per kind from yarn hairiness (`PERIOD_FUZZ`, estimates): worsted 0.25, flannel 0.5, denim 0.15, duck 0.1,
  shirting 0.05; silk and polyester none. `periodLobes` now fits grey 0.1 worsted a sheen of 0.077 (roughness 0.2) and
  flannel 0.22 (0.35). Left: a dark denim (grey 0.03) fits sheen 1.0 at roughness 0.05 with fit error 0.73, a thin rim
  only, and the fibre layer dims the weave's mirror reflection at grazing (one bounce, homogeneous slab); both want
  checking on rendered frames.
- **Regression:** packages/humans/test/cast.test.js "wool and cotton get a grazing sheen from their fibre ends;
  filament cloth gets none" (old: worsted sheen 0).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: GTAO (or SSAO) in a scene with TerrainColors gave a GPU validation error every frame (KB-POST-GTAO-TERRAINLOOK1, post)

- **Repro:** `packages/scenes/test/look-family-gpu.html` with no `skip` (a `PostStack` of GTAO, SSGI, bloom and Tonemap,
  and a heightfield mesh with `TerrainColors.attach`): the first frame threw "[Invalid CommandBuffer] is invalid due to
  a previous error"; the first uncaptured error was "Number of entries (1) did not match the expected number of entries
  (2)" for a layout of binding 0 and binding 41 (a 176 B fragment uniform), on WebGPU (RTX A6000, 2026-11-18).
- **Cause:** the ambient replay of `packages/post/src/ssao.ts` (shared by GTAO). When the lit shader had no
  `margoAmbient`, the replay cut the shader from `let direct=` and bound only bindings 18, 8 and 144 of `c.bindings`.
  TerrainColors' look uniform (binding 41) is read above `let direct=` where the material colour is made, so the
  replay pipeline's `auto` layout still held it and the bind group lacked it. A class: any plugin binding outside the
  hand-picked three. The replay now keeps the whole lit shader with the lighting in a dead `if(false)` block (as SSGI's
  and SSR's replays do) and binds all of `c.bindings`; the ambient term it returns is unchanged.
- **Regression:** packages/post/test/replay-bindings-browser.mjs (in post `test:gpu`; a test plugin's bindings above and
  below `let direct=` under SSAO, GTAO, SSGI, SSR, SceneTargets and a PostStack, and TerrainColors under GTAO; 12 and
  13 errors per case on the old code, WebGPU and MARGO_COMPAT=1), packages/post/test/ssao.test.js ("SSAO binds a plugin
  binding read above let direct="), the class check in tests/shader-contracts.test.js (no package filters a pass
  context's bindings), and packages/scenes/test/look-family-gpu.mjs, which draws the terrain under the GTAO again.

### Fixed 2026-11-18: natural after another look left a Water's chop and wind as that look set them (KB-SCENES-LOOKFAMILY-PARTS1, water)

- **Repro:** `applyWaterSettings(water, WATER_LOOKS.animatedFeature); applyWaterSettings(water, {})`: the frame uniform
  kept chop 0.12 where a fresh Water has 0, so `applyLookFamily('natural', { water })` did not give back the defaults.
- **Cause:** the `chop`, `windSpeed` and `windDirection` rows default to null (the weather's), and a null row left the
  value alone even when these rows had set it themselves. A null now hands back what the rows took: the options' chop,
  and the wind the Water had before the rows set it (the drive writes it again from then on).
- **Regression:** packages/water/test/settings.test.js ("null rows hand back a wind and a chop the rows set"), and
  packages/scenes/test/look-family-parts.test.js (every part through the family, natural byte for byte).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: the postfx GPU check's hand-built depth of field and tonemap effects predated their packages (KB-POSTFX-DOFSTALE1, scripts)

- **Repro:** `node scripts/run-with-timeout.mjs --max=10 -- node scripts/modern-postfx-tests.js` failed "Near CoC
  sign/clamp" on native WebGPU, and with `--compat` "Focused color changed" (the bokeh output read 0, 0, 0, 0 at the
  in-focus pixel), on origin/main (RTX A6000, 2026-11-18; found running `@margoengine/webgl2-compat`'s GPU tests for
  KB-COMPAT-POSTTASK1).
- **Cause:** a stale check, not an engine bug. The check builds the depth-of-field passes by hand from
  `packages/dof/src/shaders.ts`. Since the 2026-11-15 near-gather commits (d9c965dc70, a7974089bd, 40dcf8a22a) the
  bokeh shader also reads a trilinear sampler and the near mip chain (`nearTaps`, `nearShapes`, `nearScene`, bindings 6
  to 9) made by the near and near-down passes, which the check never ran; it bound 6 of 10 entries. On native WebGPU the
  invalid bind group invalidates the whole command buffer, so the depth and CoC passes never ran either and the CoC read
  back as zeros ("Near CoC"); the WebGL2 layer ran the passes it could and the bokeh pass wrote nothing. The same cause
  as the 2026-10-14 "Near CoC" failure (examples/package-benchmarks/results/gates-postfx-bisect.json, a 32-byte uniform
  after the DOF uniform grew to 48). Once bound, a second stale binding showed: the tonemap effects uniform has been 128
  bytes (the Bradford white-balance matrix, vignette colour, centre, roundness and dither) since 8b4ce98e2d, and the
  check bound 64 in the old gains layout. Its single validation error scope was popped only at the end, so each stale
  binding showed up as a wrong pixel.
- **Fix:** the check builds the near chain as `DOF` does (NEAR_LEVELS rgba16float mip levels, the near and near-down
  passes, then coarse and bokeh, in `blur()`'s order) and writes the Fx uniform in Tonemap's 32-float layout. Every
  read back first pops and reopens the validation scope, so a binding that no longer matches its package's shader fails
  with the GPU's own message. The near-edge check at x 8 asked for red above 0.999, but that pixel's 8 px disk crosses the
  foreground edge (by the thin-lens partial-occlusion model the right value is 0.991, and a 64-tap spiral cannot resolve
  under one tap, 0.016); it is replaced by a check of every pixel x 0 to 23 against the disk's covered share within two
  taps (the 64 golden-angle taps alone differ from the area by up to 1.64 taps on this edge), pure foreground where the
  disk does not reach the edge, and no far colour anywhere. Measured: within 1.2 taps at every pixel. Native WebGPU and
  `--compat` pass.
- **Regression:** the check itself (`scripts/modern-postfx-tests.js`, `npm run modern:test:postfx:browser`); with the
  near views left out of the bokeh group it now fails "GPU validation error before a read back: Number of entries (7)
  did not match the expected number of entries (10)".
- **Why no gate caught it:** check:merge selects `root/modern:test:postfx:browser` for a dof change
  (tests/check-merge-affected.test.js), but since 2026-11-10 a push runs only the changed packages' own GPU scripts, and
  this suite is a root script, so it ran after neither the dof nor the tonemap change.
- **Sources:** Potmesil and Chakravarty, "A Lens and Aperture Camera Model for Synthetic Image Generation", SIGGRAPH
  1981, https://doi.org/10.1145/965161.806818; Kraus and Strengert, "Depth-of-Field Rendering by Pyramidal Image
  Processing", Eurographics 2007, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2007.01049.x; Jimenez, "Next Generation Post
  Processing in Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare", SIGGRAPH 2014 course, https://www.iryoku.com/next-generation-post-processing-in-call-of-duty-advanced-warfare;
  Vogel, "A better way to construct the sunflower head", Mathematical Biosciences 1979,
  https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(79)90080-4.

### Fixed 2026-11-18: every fence poll of the WebGL2 layer waited about 15 ms on Windows Chrome (KB-COMPAT-POSTTASK1, webgl2-compat)

- **Repro:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node scripts/check-owner-lifetime-browser.mjs --packages=water --entry=Water
  --entry=Water.attach "--entry=Water with terrain and spray" --entry=FFTOcean`: 29.2 s on the layer against 9.9 s on
  native WebGPU (RTX A6000, ANGLE Direct3D 11, Chrome 157). water's check:owners took 505 s of its 600 s limit, the
  WebGL2 pass 354 s of case time against 124 s native (2.9 times).
- **Cause:** `nextGPUTask` (`packages/webgl2-compat/src/device/tasks.ts`), the yield between two polls of a fence for
  `onSubmittedWorkDone` and `mapAsync`, used `scheduler.postTask(fn, { delay: 1 })`. Chrome on Windows runs those
  delayed tasks on the system timer tick (15.6 ms by default; Microsoft, "timeBeginPeriod function", Win32 API
  reference): 100 yields averaged 15.1 ms each, where a port message and then `setTimeout(fn, 1)` from that task took
  2.0 ms and chained `setTimeout(fn, 1)` 4.65 ms (the HTML Standard's timer initialisation steps clamp a timer set from
  a timer, nesting level above 5, to 4 ms; the WICG Prioritized Task Scheduling draft leaves a delayed task's timing to
  the user agent). Native WebGPU signals the same waits without polling. A CPU profile of the page hid the cost: the V8
  sampler raises the Windows timer resolution, and the same four entries then took 15 s.
- **Fix:** every poll posts a port message and sets a 1 ms timer from that task (nesting level 0, so never clamped),
  still leaving the event loop idle for WebGL sync status to advance. The four entries take 13.9 s on the layer.
- **Regression test:** `packages/webgl2-compat/test/task-polling.test.js` (a page scheduler whose `postTask` fails the
  test; every poll timer is 1 ms and none is set from a timer callback).
- **Sources:** Microsoft, "timeBeginPeriod function" (Win32 API reference,
  https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/timeapi/nf-timeapi-timebeginperiod); WHATWG, HTML Living Standard,
  "Timers" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/timers-and-user-prompts.html#timers); WICG, "Prioritized Task
  Scheduling" draft (https://wicg.github.io/scheduling-apis/).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: the WebGL2 layer read getError after every allocation, a GPU-process round trip each (KB-COMPAT-GETERROR1, webgl2-compat)

- **Repro:** water's owner/lifetime cases on the layer in one page (37 entries, 481 cases, a GL call counter on the
  page): 61,489 `getError` calls, 21.4 s of a 173 s run waiting in them (0.35 ms each; RTX A6000, ANGLE Direct3D 11).
- **Cause:** `CompatDevice.allocated` (`packages/webgl2-compat/src/device/device.ts`) read `getError` after every
  buffer, texture and renderbuffer store, to report `GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY` as WebGPU's out-of-memory error. In Chrome
  `getError` waits for the GPU process to run every command before it (MDN, "WebGL best practices": avoid blocking calls
  such as getError in production).
- **Fix:** GL error flags stay set until `getError` reads them (OpenGL ES 3.0.6 specification, section 2.5 "GL
  Errors"), so one `getError` checks every allocation since the last check: in a task of its own after the first, and
  before an `out-of-memory` or `internal` scope opens or closes and before any other error is reported. The scopes that
  can catch an allocation error are the same at the allocation and at its check, so each error goes to the same scope
  as before and reaches `uncapturederror` listeners before the errors of later calls. The same run makes 13,255 calls
  (4.9 s). An error found for several allocations names them all ("one of 2 allocations (buffer 'a' ..., buffer 'b'
  ...)").
- **Regression test:** `packages/webgl2-compat/test/device.test.js` ("allocations share one getError per task or
  out-of-memory scope, each error in its own scope and order": twenty allocations in one task, one getError).
- **Sources:** Khronos, "OpenGL ES Version 3.0.6" specification, 2019, section 2.5
  (https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGLES/specs/es/3.0/es_spec_3.0.pdf); MDN, "WebGL best practices"
  (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebGL_API/WebGL_best_practices); W3C, "WebGPU", section 22 "Errors
  & Debugging" (https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#errors-and-debugging).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: an abort while BiomeView.attach loaded its parts leaked the view it had built (KB-BIOMES-ATTACH-ABORT, biomes)

- **Repro:** `BiomeView.attach(engine, world, { wetness, signal })` with the signal aborting while the plant-map imports
  (`@margoengine/scatter/states`, `@margoengine/biomes/disturbance`) load: attach rejected with the reason, but the
  terrain, its textures and every part already attached stayed alive in the scene.
- **Cause:** only the overview await and the last abort check disposed the view; the abort checks after the imports and
  every await after them (placement, objects, wet ground, water, rivers) threw straight out of attach.
- **Fix:** everything after the view is built runs in one try block; on any error or abort the view is disposed and the
  error is rethrown unchanged.
- **Regression:** `packages/biomes/tests/view-attach-abort.test.js` (the abort lands after each await in turn).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: check:owners for water alone ran past its 10 minutes with every case passing (KB-OWN-LEAVES1, scripts)

- **Repro:** `node scripts/run-with-timeout.mjs --max=10 -- npm run check:owners -- --packages=water`: exit 124 at
  600 s after the CPU model (455 passed) and 62 of the 70 browser leaves, every one 13 passed, 0 failed.
- **Cause:** water's fixture ran one browser leaf per entry (`leafPerEntry`), so its 35 entries made 70 leaves with the
  WebGL2 pass, and each leaf started its own dev server and browser and compiled the shared shaders again, about 3.5 s
  a leaf. The cases themselves take 118 s native and 294 s on the WebGL2 layer in one browser, the same within noise on
  origin/main without the sheet row 8 water commits (109 s and 304 s): main's new entries (ships, icebergs, floods) took
  the leaf count past what 10 minutes holds.
- **Fix:** a fixture may export `leafCases` (a whole number of 13-case entries, at most 208): check:owners packs its
  entries in order into leaves of at most that many cases, every entry in exactly one leaf, inside the leaf's unchanged
  180 s limit. water sets 104 (eight entries a leaf, at most 79 s on the WebGL2 layer of the workstation): 10 leaves in
  place of 70, the same cases, and the check passes in 468 s.
- **Regression test:** `tests/owner-lifetime.test.js` ("leafCases packs every entry, in order, into leaves of at most
  that many cases"; "water runs check:owners in leaves of eight entries, not one leaf per entry").

### Fixed 2026-11-18: a coast's first frame took about 7 minutes on the WebGL2 layer (KB-WATER-SURFCPU1, water)

- **Repro:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs`: the first `engine.render` of a `Water` with a
  `terrain` (a 512 x 82 coastal grid) returned after 421 s (RTX A6000, ANGLE D3D11); the test hit its 10 minute limit
  once it attached a second sea.
- **Cause:** the surf field's build (`SurfFieldBuilder` in `packages/water/src/surf.ts`) kept every entry point in one
  module whose buffer was `array<atomic<u32>>`, for the one `atomicMax` of the deepest edge. The WebGL2 layer runs any
  entry point that touches an atomic on its CPU tier, one invocation at a time, so all 594 relaxation sweeps of every
  cell ran in JavaScript.
- **Fix:** two modules over the same buffer: the deepest edge keeps its atomic; the sources and the sweeps read and
  write plain words (each invocation its own cell, from one field to the other), so the layer runs them as GPU point
  draws (its scatter tier). The field is the same: the surf check reads the same breaking depths, heights and run-up on
  both backends. Now the first frame takes 4.0 s, with 3 compute dispatches on the CPU tier.
- **Regression test:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs`: fewer than 16 CPU-tier dispatches in
  the first frame (the old build made one per sweep).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: a wind sea never broke on a beach (KB-WATER-SURFFIELD1, water)

- **Repro:** `Water` with `wind: 12` and no `waves` over a `terrain` beach: the surf shader's breaking stayed near 0 in
  the surf zone, where the same beach breaks a 1 m swell.
- **Cause:** `surfFieldK` and `fieldK` in `packages/water/src/surf.ts` took the field's wavenumber from the longest train
  with any height. A wind sea keeps its long trains with heights of 1e-31 to 1e-5 m, so the 582 m or 1,500 m train set
  the field, and every real wave counted as short chop that keeps its deep phase and never shoals or breaks.
- **Fix:** the field follows the train with the most height (the peak of the sea); one train is as before.
- **Regression tests:** `packages/water/test/breaker.test.js` (a near-empty long train leaves the breaker depth);
  `node packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs` with and without `MARGO_COMPAT=1`: a 12 m/s wind sea breaks at every
  probe inside its CPU breaker line.

### Fixed 2026-11-18: the sky and a fog volume's ambient stayed bright under the thickest smoke or ash (KB-AIR-SKYLIGHT1, weather and sky)

- **Repro:** `node packages/weather/tests/settings-check.mjs`, `volumeLoad()`: a `VolumetricFog` under the drive in
  `WEATHER_LOOKS.ashfall` read 83, 83, 80 on the far ground rows against 57, 52, 32 in clear air (RTX A6000, WebGPU;
  85, 86, 84 on the WebGL2 layer), though the ash lets through under a tenth of the light (`hazeLight`).
- **Cause:** the drive dimmed the sun (`atmosphere.sunColor`) only on a sky that had a `look` or an `atmosphere`, so a
  plain root `Sky` kept its clear dome, environment map and horizon light; and where it did dim, the dome went down by
  the direct share alone with nothing for the light the layer scatters, so a fog volume scattered the clear sky's light.
- **Fix:** the sky's new `atmosphere.scatteredLight` (`@margoengine/sky`): a low layer lit from above shines evenly over
  the day sky with the light it scatters down over pi (a share of the zenith sun on level ground), into the dome, its
  reflections, its light on the scene and the sky fog; `Sky.airControls` says a sky takes `atmosphere`. The drive gives
  such a sky an `atmosphere` under a load and writes `scatteredLight` as `hazeLight` less the direct sun times the sine of
  the sun's height (two-stream slab, Meador and Weaver 1980; the uniform overcast radiance of Moon and Spencer 1942).
  Now the far rows read clear 57, 52, 32, ash 22, 20, 8 and the sky rows clear 215, 220, 228, ash 19, 26, 33, smoke
  103, 62, 6 (WebGPU; the WebGL2 layer within 1).
- **Regression tests:** `node packages/weather/tests/settings-check.mjs`, with and without `MARGO_COMPAT=1`: the far air
  in the ash-filled volume below 0.8 and the sky over the ash fall and the wildfire smoke below 0.6 of clear air's
  luminance, and the layer light written; `packages/sky/test/look.test.js` (the light rides the look block and the day
  sky adds it).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: the haze colour was lit at full light under the thickest smoke or ash (KB-AIR-HAZELIGHT1, weather)

- **Repro:** `packages/weather/tests/settings-check.html` `airLoad()`: under `WEATHER_LOOKS.ashDarkness` (about 180 m)
  the lit ground row read 60, 61, 58 against 30, 27, 15 under `ashfall`; the same under `blackDay` against
  `wildfireSmoke` (34, 29, 12 against 30, 24, 4). Real air under a thick layer goes dark.
- **Cause:** `WeatherDrive.tintFog` in `packages/weather/src/drive.ts` set the sky fog's colour to the haze's diffusion
  albedo times `dustLight`, `smokeLight`, `ashLight` or `sprayLight`, a fixed light; nothing lowered it for the sunlight
  and skylight that reach into a thick layer, so the fog in front of everything was as bright as in a thin haze.
- **Fix:** the new `hazeLight(state, elevation)` in `packages/weather/src/air.ts` is the light that still reaches the air:
  the direct sun through the layers plus the scattered rest times a two-stream slab's transmission (Meador and Weaver
  1980), and the drive multiplies the fog colour by it (the airlight of Koschmieder 1924 is the in-scattered light).
  Now the lit ground reads clear 54, 48, 24, ash fall 26, 22, 3, darkness 24, 20, 2; smoke haze 46, 36, 6, wildfire
  29, 23, 3, black day 25, 21, 2, the same on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (RTX A6000).
- **Regression tests:** `packages/weather/tests/air-load.test.js` (the fog colour darkens at every step of smoke, ash and
  spray, and is the colour times `hazeLight`); `node packages/weather/tests/settings-check.mjs`, with and without
  `MARGO_COMPAT=1`: the lit ground and the far haze rows darken at every step from clear to a black day and to the ash
  darkness.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: the inside of a shed on the dune coast is as bright as the open sand (KB-SCENES-SKYOCC1, environment, sky)

- **Repro:** `node packages/scenes/test/dune-coast-still.mjs --w=1920 --h=1080 --out=<folder> --shots=<file>` with a shot
  `asset=/asset-library/kitty-hawk/hangar-1903/hangar-1903.glb&camp=0&at=0,-30&eye=9.8,1.8,3.8&look=6.7,1.9,0`:
  the sand floor and the far wall inside the open hangar are lit like the sand outside.
- **Cause:** under the overcast sky nearly all light is sky light, and the sky's light (`lighting.ambient`: nine
  spherical harmonics and the sky map) lit every surface with the whole sky, with no visibility term; the screen-space
  occlusion (1.5 m) cannot shut out a roof 2 m up. `LightProbes` already had visibility (an irradiance volume baked from
  the scene, Chebyshev bins) and saw the sky through `addCapture(sky)`, but once attached it owned the ambient term
  and lit everything outside its volume with core's flat ambient instead of the sky: the open sand lost about a
  quarter of its light (0.0766 against 0.1006), so no scene could use it for this.
- **Fix:** `LightProbes` takes `sky` (`@margoengine/environment/probes`): outside the volume the sky's own
  `skyIrradiance` and `skyRadiance` (a new sky WGSL function beside `skyLighting`, which is unchanged) light the scene
  exactly as the sky does alone; inside, the sky light comes only through what the probes see of it; the sky is
  captured for you. README "Sky light indoors" has the example and sources. The dune-coast scene itself is not changed
  here (scene work is held): a scene puts a volume over each shed or room.
- **Regression:** `packages/environment/tests/sky-occlusion-browser.js` (`npm run test:sky-occlusion:browser`, WebGPU
  and `--compat`): a 4 m shed lit only through its door and two windows under the overcast preset; the floor against
  the open sand is 1.0 with the sky alone, 0.093 with the probes and `sky`, 0.017 shut, and the sand keeps 0.1006
  exactly (before the fix: 0.0766, failing). `packages/environment/tests/probes.test.js` checks the patch, the
  bindings and the validation on a mock GPU.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: on the WebGL2 layer a PlantStates map composed on the layer's CPU tier every frame (KB-STATES-COMPOSECPU1, scatter)

- **Repro:** `planCompute({ source: composeShader })` (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat/compute`, `composeShader` of
  `@margoengine/scatter/states`) planned the compose pass on the `cpu` tier ("an invocation reads back 'map' after
  storing to it"): JavaScript for every map cell each frame (65,536 at the default resolution), with a read-back.
- **Cause:** invocation 0 wrote the map's two header words and then read the map's cells, a read after its own store,
  which the layer's analysis sends to its CPU tier. The CPU already writes the header when it makes the map, so the
  store was extra work.
- **Fix:** the pass only reads the header and stores each cell after its last read; the layer runs it as a point draw
  on the GPU (`scatter` tier).
- **Regression:** `packages/scatter/test/states.test.js` ("the compose pass runs as a GPU draw on the WebGL2 layer").

### Fixed 2026-11-17: on the WebGL2 layer effects with over-life ran their kernels on the CPU tier, and every step ran before the route loaded (KB-VFX-EMBERCPU1, vfx)

- **Repro:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node scripts/test-pages-browser.mjs --page=plant-states`: the first button click took 100 to
  113 s (95 s under `VFX` `simulate` in the layer's `runCPU`, kernels `main`, `deaths` and `scan`).
- **Cause:** two things. (1) `VFX` encoded its steps in the first frames, before the route's `import()` had resolved
  (`VFX.route` unset), so the layer ran the WebGPU kernels of each one, and the effects of a flame (a prewarm of 600
  steps each) took the CPU tier's workgroup scans. (2) Once the route was set its `update` kernel of an effect with
  `overLife` still planned on the CPU tier ("an invocation reads back 'particles' after storing to it"): over-life read
  `particles[cold+1].z` and `lifeBirth[i]` back after the birth block stored to them (22 s of the 25 s that were left).
- **Fix:** while the route loads, a `VFX` with a prewarm keeps each frame's steps (prewarm and live step, as counted) and
  runs them in order on the route's draws when it resolves (`reset` and `dispose` drop them); an effect with no prewarm
  still simulates every frame on its WebGPU kernels until then, as `loadCompatRoute` promises (holding those too left
  the ribbons of `packages/vfx/test/features-check.mjs` undrawn on the WebGL2 layer); over-life reads the stored life and
  birth velocity into locals before the slot stores anything, so the route's kernels plan as GPU draws. The page's
  first click no longer shows in the runner's slow-click note.
- **Regression:** `packages/vfx/test/route-loading.test.js` (no prewarm simulated before the route loads and its steps
  run after it; an effect with no prewarm simulates every frame meanwhile; no route kernel of an over-life effect plans
  on the `cpu` tier).

### Accepted 2026-11-17: on the WebGL2 layer over ANGLE Direct3D 11 the same calls draw 3 sea pixels one code apart a few seconds in (KB-WATER-SETTINGS-COMPAT1, water, webgl2-compat; driver)

- **Repro:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node packages/water/test/frame-repeat.browser.mjs` (RTX A6000, NVIDIA 617.42, Edge 157,
  ANGLE Direct3D 11): a still sea drawn with `delta: 0` and no value changed, one frame every 300 ms, draws 3 pixels one
  code apart (7,70,84 to 8,70,84 and two more, all in the sea) about 1 to 6 s after its first frame, in the drawing
  buffer before the canvas shows it (a `readPixels` of the layer's context), and then mostly keeps them, now and then
  flipping back. `packages/water/test/settings.browser.mjs` failed on it ("whitecaps at its default does not bring the
  frame back") when one of its later frames landed past that mark. Native WebGPU never moves, nor does the layer on
  ANGLE Vulkan (`BROWSER_ARGS='["--use-angle=vulkan"]'`) or on ANGLE's Direct3D 11 WARP software device on the same PC.
- **Cause:** inside the Direct3D 11 driver, not in Margo. Every WebGL2 call the layer makes was recorded with its
  arguments and a hash of every uploaded byte (`tests/support/gl-stream.js`): a frame before the change and a frame
  after it make the same 169 calls with the same data, and no WebGL2 call runs between frames. Water's 140 uniform
  floats are bit for bit the same, and the pixels move with a single-sampled scene too, so it is not only the 4x MSAA
  repeatability loss of batch 160 (docs/limits.md). The same calls with the same data give other pixels only on the
  hardware Direct3D 11 driver, which compiles shaders on its own schedule and may replace a binary it already runs;
  the rounding of one float32 operation is enough to move a pixel one code. A plain WebGL2 page with a long
  transcendental shader did not move over 60 s, so it shows with some programs only. The layer cannot fix it: it already
  hands the driver the same work.
- **Accepted:** frames the water checks require to be equal are held to the same WebGL2 calls and data on the layer
  (any back end), and to the same pixels on WebGPU and on the layer everywhere except ANGLE Direct3D 11, where the pixel
  count is printed instead. Expect a few pixels one code apart between two frames seconds apart on that device.
- **Regression:** `packages/water/test/frame-repeat.browser.mjs` (34 frames over 10 s: the same pixels on WebGPU and
  ANGLE Vulkan, the same WebGL2 calls on the layer); a water build that changes a uniform after 5 s of wall time fails
  it on WebGPU (pixels) and on ANGLE Direct3D 11 (another `bufferSubData` hash at frame 6), checked 2026-11-17.
  `packages/water/test/settings.browser.mjs` compares calls the same way and passes on all three.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: a transparent past VolumetricFog's range got the fog only up to range (KB-FOG-FAR-TRANSPARENT, environment)

- **Repro:** `VolumetricFog.attach(engine, {visibility: 1000, range: 600})` with a pane added by `fog.add(pane)` on a
  sea 1 km out: the sea showed 2% contrast (Koschmieder) and the pane 9.6%, the fog of its first 600 m.
- **Cause:** `margoTransparentAt` in `packages/environment/src/volumetric.ts` read the froxel volume at the fragment's
  depth clamped to `range`; the analytic far air (`tailDepth`, `farLight`) ran only in the composite, for opaque depth.
- **Fix:** the far air's WGSL is one shared text (`farAir`) the composite and `margoTransparentAt` both compile; past
  `range` a fogged transparent adds the same closed-form tail, lit from the sky map (two new hook bindings, 123 and 124,
  a 1 x 1 blank without a sky). Regression: `packages/environment/tests/volumetric-far.browser.mjs` (a pane on the sea
  within 0.01 of the integral past range, 2.07% contrast at V, and with a Sky within 1% of the fogged sea under it; the
  old shader is off by 0.095), WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: the sky's ambient beside an EnvironmentLighting lost the GPU (KB-ENV-AMBIENT-DUP1, sky)

- **Repro:** `Sky.attach(engine, sunlitSky())` (which sets `lighting.ambient`) and `EnvironmentLighting.load(engine,
  'workshop.hdr')` on one engine: the scene shader declared `let margoAmbient=` twice (`skyLighting` and `iblShade`),
  WGSL refused it ("redeclaration of 'margoAmbient'") and every mesh drew black.
- **Cause:** the sky patched core's shader in its lighting pass at order -6, before the scene effects that patch at -1,
  so an explicit environment found the sky's term already there and added its own.
- **Fix:** the sky's light map is still drawn at -6, but its shader patch waits for `sky:environment` at -0.5 and is
  left out when an explicit environment (EnvironmentLighting, LightProbes) has already written `margoAmbient`: the
  environment owns the ambient, the sky keeps the sun and moon. Regression: `packages/sky/test/sky.test.js` (one
  `margoAmbient`, no sky bindings beside the environment's) and `packages/sky/test/sky-environment-check.mjs` (a real
  HDR on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer; it also shows a glTF box under the sky alone draws exactly as a core box of the
  same grey, so the dark library props of the flood shots are their own dark albedo, about 0.04 linear).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: a skinned or morphed glTF primitive over 262,144 vertices was refused instead of split into parts (KB-GLTF-SKINSPLIT1, gltf, animation, exporters, lod, shader)

- **Repro:** load a skinned or morphed primitive of more than 262,144 vertices with `@margoengine/gltf/pbr` (strand hair
  on a rigged person; `splitSkinGrid(520, 520)` in `tests/support/split-skin-fixture.js`, 270,400 vertices): `MargoError`
  `unsupported`, "Skinned or morphed glTF primitive has 270400 vertices, over maxPartVertices (262144); only static
  primitives split into parts". The film asset builder had to split hair by hand.
- **Cause:** 262,144 is gltf/pbr's default `maxPartVertices` (2^18 vertices of 80 B, 20 MiB). Every packed vertex buffer
  is also bound as a storage buffer (picking, deformation), so a part must stay inside the device's
  `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` (128 MiB by WebGPU default, 64 MiB on the WebGL2 layer's 2048 context); that is why
  large primitives split, and a better layout does not remove the need (a 1,000,000-vertex whole is 80 MB, past the
  layer's binding). Static primitives already split; skinned and morphed ones were refused because every reader of
  the definition's per-vertex accessors indexed them by the part's own vertex number: `@margoengine/animation` (the
  GPU deformation's influences and morph deltas, `bakeVAT`, `bakeBones`), `@margoengine/exporters` (`exportModel`'s
  morph targets, the scene collector's joints, weights, morphs and later UV sets), `@margoengine/shader`
  (`skinningFromModel`) and `@margoengine/lod` (a level of a split primitive, whose vertices count the parts merged
  whole, read the skin at the merged number). The animation arena also shared influence and delta blocks between
  copies by definition and vertex count, so two parts of one definition with the same count shared one block.
- **Fix:** gltf/pbr splits skinned and morphed primitives like static ones. Skinning and morphing are functions of one
  vertex's own attributes (glTF 2.0 sections 3.7.2.2 and 3.7.3; linear blend skinning as in Magnenat-Thalmann,
  Laperriere and Thalmann 1988 and Lewis, Cordner and Fong 2000; dual quaternion skinning, Kavan et al. 2008; blend
  shapes, Lewis et al. 2014), so a vertex copied onto a cut deforms identically in each part. Every reader takes the
  part's values through `part.vertexMap` (`packages/shared/vertex-map.js`, gathered once per map and accessor); the
  arena keys a part's blocks by its vertex map; lod keeps the merged whole's source vertices and composes them into
  each level's. Each part keeps the node's skin, morph weights and material. Sources: Khronos glTF 2.0 specification,
  https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html; Magnenat-Thalmann, Laperriere, Thalmann 1988,
  "Joint-dependent local deformations for hand animation and object grasping", Graphics Interface; Lewis, Cordner, Fong 2000,
  "Pose Space Deformation", SIGGRAPH, https://doi.org/10.1145/344779.344862; Kavan, Collins, Zara, O'Sullivan 2008,
  "Geometric Skinning with Approximate Dual Quaternion Blending", ACM TOG 27(4), https://doi.org/10.1145/1409625.1409627;
  Lewis, Anjyo, Rhee, Zhang, Pighin, Deng 2014, "Practice and Theory of Blendshape Facial Models", Eurographics State
  of the Art Reports; and the splitting papers cited in `packages/gltf/src/parts.ts` (Hoppe 1999, Sander et al. 2007,
  Isenburg and Lindstrom 2005, Karis et al. 2021).
- **Regression:** `packages/animation/tests/split-skin.test.js` (270,400 vertices load as parts and bake the same VAT
  bit for bit as the hand-split mesh and as the whole primitive at each part's vertices; uploaded influences and morph
  deltas equal the hand-split mesh's; two equal-count parts keep their own blocks), `packages/gltf/test/parts.test.js`
  ("a skinned, morphed primitive over the default part size splits and draws as the mesh split by hand"),
  `packages/exporters/tests/split-skin.test.js`, `packages/shader/test/deform.test.js` ("a part of a primitive gltf/pbr
  split reads the joints and weights of its own vertices"), `packages/lod/test/auto.test.js` ("a real Fox split into
  parts"), and the GPU check `packages/gltf/scripts/test-skinned-parts-browser.mjs` (`npm run test:gpu:skinned-parts`
  in packages/gltf): the parts' deformed vertices equal the hand-split primitives' and the whole primitive's bit for
  bit, and the two models draw the same pixels, natively and on the WebGL2 layer (RTX A6000, 2026-11-17).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: on the WebGL2 layer the page canvas showed nothing in the task of a scene's first compute submit (KB-COMPAT-FIRSTTASK1, webgl2-compat)

- **Repro:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node scripts/run-with-timeout.mjs --max=10 -- node packages/sky/test/rain-frames-check.mjs`:
  its leg that reads the page canvas in the same task as `engine.render()` gets frame 0 all zero (transparent black),
  frames 1 to 89 equal to the headless frames. Any `Sky` is enough (bruneton or preetham, everything else off); a page
  without compute shows its first frame. Two renders in one task are both blank; a 500 ms wait before the first render,
  or an `await` of `device.queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()` after it, shows the frame.
- **Cause:** the layer loads its compute part (`compute/runtime.js`, by `import()`) at the first `createComputePipeline`,
  and `queue.submit` holds every submit from then on until it has loaded (`CompatQueue.hold`). The sky makes its
  compute pipelines inside its first frame, so that frame's commands, and the canvas present that ends them, run after
  the task; WebGPU shows a canvas texture to a read in the same task. Frames still run in order, so `readPixels`,
  `mapAsync` and anything that waits for the GPU see the right frame, and `rain-frames-check.mjs` pins that the
  blank is frame 0 only. A synchronous `capture` in `@margoengine/exporters` of a scene's first compute frame on the
  layer gives the blank too. Fix options (needs a maintainer decision): load the compute part in `requestDevice`
  (about 27 KB more for every layer page, compute or not), or a package builds its compute pipelines when attached.
- **Fix:** `requestDevice` of the layer loads the compute part before it answers (the way it already loads the read-back
  part for a lower tier), so no submit waits in the queue for it and the first render's canvas present runs in its
  own task. A render-only page downloads the compute chunk too (the chunk stays out of the entry; the
  `basic-scene-network` record notes the added request).
- **Regression:** `packages/webgl2-compat/test/compute-first-submit.test.js` (fails on the old layer) and
  `packages/sky/test/rain-frames-check.mjs`, whose page-canvas leg now expects frame 0 to equal the headless frame.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: wall-clock millisecond budgets made what a frame draws depend on machine speed (KB-FILM-CLOCK1; terrain, biomes, gltf, post)

- **Repro:** a fake slow `performance.now` (50 ms a read) against a fast one (0.001 ms): `PlanetTerrain` with the default
  4 ms budget built 1 patch a frame instead of 3 and drew other patches; `BiomeView` copied 1 arrived tile a frame instead
  of all 16; `loadGLTFProgressive` took 1 upload step a pump instead of a burst; `SceneFade` faded by wall time.
- **Cause:** each loop stopped on `performance.now() - start < budget` (terrain/src/planet.ts, biomes/src/view.ts,
  gltf/src/progressive.ts) or read the wall clock for the fade (post/src/scene-fade.ts), so the state of a frame followed
  the machine. tiles' `fade` already took a clock.
- **Fix:** `maxBuilds`, `maxSteps` and `maxJobs`, work counts that replace the millisecond budget, and a `clock` option on
  each (`SceneFade.attach(engine, duration, clock)`). The live defaults are unchanged.
- **Regression:** `packages/terrain/test/planet.test.js`, `packages/biomes/tests/view-clock.test.js`,
  `packages/gltf/test/progressive.test.js`, `tests/modern-scene-fade-lifecycle.test.js` (each fails on the old build).

### Corrected 2026-11-17: fresh runs of a film's rain shot seemed to draw whole frames differently (GAP-FILM-READY, KB-FILM-GPUSHARE1)

- **Repro:** a page that draws the shot (Bruneton sky with clouds, AgX, shadows, rain), awaits
  `queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()` and then copies the WebGPU canvas with `drawImage`: two fresh runs differed in 65 of
  90 frames, whole frames, and a still frame read black for its first 2 to 13 draws.
- **Cause:** the read, not the engine. After an `await` the canvas gives the last frame the browser showed, which lags
  by a number of frames that differs per process. Read with `readPixels` on `createHeadlessCanvas`, or in the same task
  as the render, the shot is byte for byte the same in every fresh run from frame 0, alone and beside a second process
  keeping the GPU busy (2 alone and 3 shared runs of 240 frames, 4 runs of 90 frames on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer).
  No package's asynchronous pipeline compile leaves a frame half drawn: core awaits its two, gltf's `compile()`,
  `RawShaders.ready()` and the other `create*PipelineAsync` callers await theirs or draw with a pipeline made at once.
  Regression: `packages/sky/test/rain-frames-check.mjs` (in the sky `test:gpu`); docs:
  [headless README](../packages/headless/README.md#the-same-frames-on-every-run).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: Caustics and the surface capture compiled the water surface three times a stage, past check:owners' wait on the WebGL2 layer (KB-WATER-SURFCOMPILE1, water)

- **Repro:** `MARGO_COMPAT=1 node scripts/check-owner-lifetime-browser.mjs --packages=water "--entry=PostStack of
  Caustics and Underwater"` (also `"--entry=Caustics.attach"`) on the parent commit: "not ready after about 22 s, 0
  pipelines compiling". `node packages/water/test/surface-copies.browser.mjs` fails there: fieldVertex, probeVertex,
  beamVertex and measure each hold 3 copies of `surface()`.
- **Cause:** Caustics' `beamVertex` and `measure` and the surface capture's `rectangle` (its field and probe stages)
  called `surface()` once per triangle corner, three call sites. A shader compiler inlines every call; on the WebGL2
  layer ANGLE's D3D11 backend hands the HLSL to FXC, and each copy of the swell, surf and coast costs it about 1.5 s.
  Timed on this PC (RTX A6000, ANGLE D3D11): those four programs took 3.9, 4.6, 4.9 and 4.6 s, and the first frame
  of Water with Caustics and Underwater 22 to 26 s, so the surf's extra terms tipped it past the 20 s wait. The layer
  compiles each distinct GLSL program once per device already (`LinkedProgram`); the copies were in the WGSL itself.
- **Fix:** the three corners come from one call in a loop (`for k in 0..3`), so each stage compiles one copy. The
  same programs take 1.7, 1.7, 2.3 and 2.0 s and the first frame 13.7 s; native WebGPU 2.2 to 4.3 s before, 1.5 to
  2.7 s after. The values are unchanged. Regression: `packages/water/test/surface-copies.browser.mjs` (in `test:gpu`)
  counts the inlined `surface()` copies of every entry point the device was asked for, from its WGSL.

### Fixed 2026-11-18: a flood wave lost about 3% of its height every 50 m over open water (KB-FLOOD-DAMP1, water)

- **Repro:** a `Flood` strip over 10 m of water, 2 m cells, a wave maker of 0.1 m and 8 s (40 cells a wavelength): the
  train fell from 0.0984 m 19 m ahead to 0.0839 m at 269 m. On the CPU reference a 0.1 m simple-wave hump of 9 cells
  over a flat frictionless bed lost 10.7% of its crest in 100 m and 27.2% in 500 m, where the exact crest keeps its height.
- **Cause:** the scheme's order at crests and troughs. Minmod slopes are 0 at every extremum, so each crest was
  reconstructed piecewise constant and the HLL flux's dissipation acted on a first-order jump there. Not the cause
  (each measured on the reference): the time step (Courant 0.25 against 0.04 changed the 500 m loss by 0.2 points), friction
  (none in the test) or the sea side (none on the reference); the HLL flux's dissipation for these slow waves is about
  c / 2 times the jump at the face, as Roe's, so it is as large as the reconstruction leaves the jump. Less clipping limiters still clip: generalised minmod theta 1.3
  and 2 lost 15.7% and 9.4% in 500 m, Koren's third-order limiter 8.5%, WENO3 22.8%, WENO3-Z 15.9%; unlimited third-order
  faces lost 3.0%, so a wider stencil was needed.
- **Fix:** fifth-order WENO-Z face values of h, w = h + b, u and v (Borges, Carmona, Costa, Don 2008, with Castro, Costa,
  Don 2011's power 2) wherever all five cells of the stencil hold more than 1 cm and both depth faces stay at or above 0;
  minmod as before at shorelines, fronts and the edges of a wet patch, so positivity, the wall mirror and every wet/dry
  bound hold as they were. The hydrostatic reconstruction keeps the lake at rest for any reconstruction (Audusse et al.
  2004; Noelle, Xing, Shu 2007 for WENO). Walls now mirror two cells (the stencil reads three out), open and sea sides
  copy the edge cell. Measured: the 500 m crest loss is 0.65% on the reference; on the GPU (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer)
  the maker's train goes from 0.0997 m at 219 m to 0.0984 m at 469 m (0.26% per 50 m) and a solitary tsunami's crest
  from 0.0985 m at 60 m to 0.0983 m at 568 m (0.16%).
  Regression: `packages/water/test/flood-bounds.test.js` (the simple wave: crest within 1% after 100, 250 and 500 m, in
  place within half a cell; fails on the old reference at 100 m with 10.7%) and `packages/water/test/flood-waves.browser.mjs`
  (the solitary tsunami's crest within 1% over 500 m, `test:gpu`; the old kernel lost 20.1%). The Thacker, Ritter, Stoker, bore, jump, run-up,
  lake-at-rest, volume and wall bounds are unchanged and pass.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: a flood's sea side sent the sea in at 40 to 57 m/s over a nearly dry edge (KB-FLATHER-DRY1, water)

- **Repro:** a 64 x 32 map of 2 m cells, its east side 'sea', half a 10 m channel and half land 1.7 m over the sea
  falling inland, and a 7 m trough-first tsunami: under the crest the channel spreads thin sheets over the land edge and
  the sea side drives them at 57 m/s against the flood's 20 m/s limit, 513 cells capped. Found in a 1 km harbour test
  map at 40 m/s, 84 cells capped, all on the land at the sea side.
- **Cause:** the sea side was Flather's linear condition with sqrt(g / h) taken at the edge cell's own depth: the
  ghost's current a sqrt(g / h) + sqrt(g / h) (eta_out - eta_in) grows like h^-1/2 as the edge cell dries, and its momentum
  flux h u^2 does not vanish with h. The linearisation holds only for a wave small against the depth (Blayo and Debreu
  2005); a dry edge also mirrored like a wall, so the sea could not come back over it.
- **Fix:** the nonlinear form, from the Riemann invariants (`seaGhost` in `packages/water/src/flood-shaders.ts`): the
  incoming invariant u + 2 sqrt(g h) is the outer sea's, the outgoing one the edge cell's; supercritical inflow takes
  the outer sea as the ghost and the Riemann solver makes the front (at most 2 sqrt(g h), Ritter 1892). The repro map
  peaks at 15.7 m/s with no cell capped (the harbour map at 17.5 m/s); the other sea-side bounds hold (a leaving wave 0.01%, a lake at rest exact).
  Regression: `packages/water/test/flood-sea.browser.mjs` case 9 (in `test:gpu`, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: a flood's sea side sent back a third of every wave leaving through it (KB-FLATHER-GHOST1, water)

- **Repro:** a `Flood` strip of 10 m water with both ends `'sea'` and a train of 0.1 m, 8 s waves running east: the
  amplitude along the strip went 0.102, 0.085, 0.104, 0.058 m, a standing wave of 1.8 : 1 from the east side.
- **Cause:** the Flather ghost cell held the outer depth with the Flather current. For a wave leaving, the HLL flux
  then saw a jump in depth the wave never had, and the steady balance of its mass flux gives a reflection of -1/3. The
  sea-side bound only measured what was left after both sides had let everything out, so it passed.
- **Fix:** the ghost holds the inside depth with the Flather current (`seaGhost` in
  `packages/water/src/flood-shaders.ts`), so the face flux of a leaving wave is its own and an arriving wave still comes
  in at its height. Measured at 469 m: the part running back is 5e-6 of 0.0839 m (0.01%).
  Regression: `packages/water/test/flood-waves.browser.mjs` (in `test:gpu`, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer) splits the
  train near the sea side into its right- and left-running parts and bounds the left one under 3%.

### Fixed 2026-11-17: the sky's light map and the engine sun were not in one unit (KB-SKY-SUNUNITS1, sky)

- **Repro:** `Sky.attach(engine, sunlitSky({elevation: degrees(60), intensity: 1}))` over a level grey plate: the sky's
  light map gave the plate 0.61 of its light (Bruneton 0.56), 1.5 times the sun's, where clear skies measure 0.1 to 0.2
  (Erbs, Klein and Duffie 1982); at intensity 3 the share fell to 0.34, because only the sun followed the intensity.
- **Cause:** the map (diffuse harmonics and reflections) lit the scene in the sky model's own radiance scale, the engine
  sun in `lighting.intensity`'s, with no factor between them.
- **Fix:** `Sky.lightScale`, the intensity over the zenith sun on the ground in sky units (Preetham 4 pi x 0.55, the
  clouds' calibration to the clear diffuse share; Bruneton 20 times the zenith transmittance), rides in the light
  buffer's last float, and `skyLighting` and `BlownSand` scale the map by it; the floor stays in engine units. The
  clouds' deck light with `dimLight: false` is now matched in the map's units. Measured shares at 60 degrees, turbidity
  2: Preetham 0.184, Bruneton 0.064, within 0.01 from intensity 1 to 3. Regression: `packages/sky/test/sky.test.js`
  (the scale per model and intensity in the buffer and the shader) and `packages/sky/test/sky-light-units-check.mjs`
  (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer: fails on the old code at 0.61).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: a flame showed no heat shimmer (KB-FLAME-HEATHAZE1, post, vfx)

- **Repro (before):** any `Flame` (or a `FireFront`'s flames) in front of a far ridge: the ridge behind the flames and the
  air over them did not ripple, as the hot plume over a real fire bends the light (USFS photos, lane E .lane/fire-refs).
- **Cause:** heat shimmer is refraction of what lies behind the plume, and nothing drew it: a frame-graph pass gets the
  colour target only as a view to draw into, so the flame could not read the scene behind it.
- **Fix:** `HeatHaze` of `@margoengine/post/heat-haze`, an HDR `PostStack` stage, which already reads the scene capture
  and its depth (no core change). Each pixel's ray is bent by the refractive field of the plumes it crosses
  (Gladstone-Dale with McCaffrey's plume temperatures, eddies at 0.4 of the mean rise), each bend weighed 1 - t / tb
  against the depth, so a surface in front of the plume never moves. `Flame.plume` gives the plume (base, length,
  footprint, lean, clock); `heatHaze.*` rows sit in `POST_SETTINGS`. Pinned by packages/post/test/heat-haze.test.js
  (the bend against a fine quadrature of the Gaussian plume within 3%) and heat-haze-browser.mjs (WebGPU and the WebGL2
  layer: the bars behind a plume move, nothing outside its column and nothing on a box in front of it, strength 0 is the
  frame with the effect off, two times differ).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: on a skinned primitive a mesh-axis `hair()` direction followed the node, not the joints (KB-MODELFEAT-JOINTS1, materials)

- **Repro:** in packages/materials/test/features.html, a sphere skinned to one joint turned 90 degrees with
  `hair({direction: [x, y, z]})` keeps its strands along the node's axis, not the joint's.
- **Cause:** the feature sets its axis in the vertex stage from `margoObjectModel`, the primitive's node (or instance)
  matrix. Skinning runs before the draw (`@margoengine/animation` writes the deformed vertices), so the vertex stage
  never sees a joint matrix. A UV-direction hair (the default) reads the deformed tangents and is right.
- **Fixed for the eye 2026-11-18:** `eye({follow})` reads a matrix on every draw that moves its centre and axis, and
  `@margoengine/humans` `addPerson` / `personEye` pass the eye joint's skin matrix. Pinned by the `modelFeatures` job of
  packages/materials/test/features-browser.mjs (eye with the joint moved 0.5 matches the moved mesh within 0 levels;
  254 levels without `follow`).
- **Fixed for hair 2026-11-18:** `hair({direction: [x, y, z], follow})` turns its direction by a matrix read on every
  draw (binding 135), and `addPerson` passes the skin matrix of the joint that carries most of the hair's weight when
  its `hair` direction is three numbers. One joint, as for the eye: a mesh-axis direction is one direction per mesh, so
  per-vertex skinning would need each vertex's rest tangent frame or its joints in the vertex stage, which the deformed
  vertices do not carry; hair over several joints runs along its UVs, whose skinned tangents already turn per vertex.
  Pinned by `modelFeatures` (hair with its joint turned 90 degrees matches the turned mesh within 0 levels, WebGPU and
  MARGO_COMPAT=1; 143 levels without `follow`), features.test.js "a mesh-axis hair direction turns with a follow
  matrix" and packages/humans/test/person-still.mjs (`addPerson` wires it on a skinned figure).

### Fixed 2026-11-17: the Bruneton sky's glow round the sun had an edge about 45 degrees out (KB-SKY-NU-EDGE1, sky)

- **Repro (before):** `node packages/sky/test/features-check.mjs settings` builds packages/sky/test/settings-check.html;
  open it with `?w=1280&h=720&ground=full` and apply `{'sun.mode': 'angles', 'sun.elevation': 25, timeScale: 0, model:
  'bruneton', turbidity: 6}`: the bright haze round the sun ended in two near vertical edges about 45 degrees either
  side of it, where a real aureole fades smoothly. A low sun (`SKY_LOOKS.sunset`) showed the same edges on its band.
- **Cause:** the Bruneton table (packages/sky/src/bruneton.ts `coordinates` and `lookup`) holds 8 samples of `nu`,
  the cosine of the angle to the sun, evenly spaced from -1 to 1, and stored scattering with the phase functions
  already applied. The two samples nearest the sun are `nu` 1 and 0.714 (0 and 44.4 degrees), and the Cornette-Shanks
  Mie phase at g 0.8 falls by a factor of about 30 between them, so the linear blend drew a straight ramp inside 44
  degrees and a slope break at it.
- **Fix:** single scattering is stored without its phase functions, Rayleigh and Mie apart (rows 256 to 767 of the
  table the sky reads, 128 x 768), and the phases are applied per pixel (`brunetonSky`) and per direction in the first
  density and ground irradiance passes; the stored values change slowly with `nu`, so the blend is smooth. Higher
  orders keep their phase, as the paper does. The per-pixel Mie phase reads its `g` from the Frame's free `clouds.w`
  (0.8, or the look's `mieAnisotropy`) so the plain and look programs stay equal pixel for pixel; the look check's
  "a high asymmetry tightens the glow" now measures the glow's shape (2.85 times brighter within 2 degrees of the sun
  at g 0.9 than at 0.2, and dimmer beyond 30 degrees), because its old band mean was raised by this very smear. Sources: E. Bruneton and F. Neyret, "Precomputed Atmospheric
  Scattering", Computer Graphics Forum 27(4), 2008, sec. 4 (https://hal.inria.fr/inria-00288758); O. Elek,
  "Rendering Parametrizable Planetary Atmospheres with Multiple Scattering in Real-Time", CESCG 2009
  (https://old.cescg.org/CESCG-2009/papers/PragueCUNI-Elek-Oskar.pdf); S. Hillaire, "A Scalable and Production Ready
  Sky and Atmosphere Rendering Technique", Computer Graphics Forum 39(4), 2020
  (https://diglib.eg.org/handle/10.1111/cgf14050), which applies the phase per sample. A denser `nu` near 1 was
  ruled out: it only narrows the ramp, and the peak at g 0.8 would need far more samples to blend without a break.
- **Regression:** `features-check.mjs settings` reads the plain Bruneton glow beside a sun 40 degrees up and bounds the
  change of its slope per degree from 8 to 58 degrees below 2.5 levels: 5.69 at 44 degrees before, 1.10 after, native
  and `MARGO_COMPAT=1`.

### Fixed 2026-11-18: the swash ran up a few centimetres where real beaches run up decimetres, and started late (KB-WATER-SWASH1, water)

- **Repro:** `node packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs` prints the run-up: a 1 m, 60 m swell on a 1:50 beach (1:28
  above the waterline) runs up 0.014 m above still water after 20 s. Stockdon et al. 2006 ("Empirical
  parameterization of setup, swash, and runup", Coastal Engineering 53(7), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coastaleng.2005.12.005)
  gives about 0.4 m for that beach and swell. In `examples/dune-coast` (four trains) the flow runs up 0.076 m, wetting
  about 2 m of sand, and only after about 20 s: the cells shallower than 0.35 m start still and the first bores take
  that long to cross them, so a still taken in the first seconds shows no swash and no wet sand.
- **Cause:** Water's coast flow (`src/coastal.ts`) was a virtual pipe: each cell's outflow was driven by the cell's
  own depth alone, no momentum was carried from face to face, and every flow decayed by 0.12 a second. A bore reaching
  the shoreline could not carry its momentum up the sand: on the NOAA solitary-wave case (Synolakis 1987,
  https://doi.org/10.1017/S002211208700329X, R / d = 0.0861 on 1:19.85 at H / d = 0.0185) that step runs up 0.0129,
  85% short (0.0228 without the decay). A 1D replica of the beach with the surf's forcing showed the same split: the
  pipe 0.042 m, a second-order finite-volume solver (test/flood-reference.js) 0.293 m frictionless and 0.153 m with
  Manning 0.02. And the flow started at rest: a long wave takes 2 sqrt(h0 / g) / slope, 19 s on 1:50, to cross from the
  0.35 m hand-over to the shoreline, so the swash began about 20 s in. Ruled out as before: the hand-over depth
  (driving the flow down to 0.1 m with the new step still damps the swash, 0.07 m in the replica).
- **Fix:** the coast flow is the shallow-water momentum equation on the same staggered grid, in the momentum-conservative
  q-form of Stelling and Duinmeijer 2003 (https://doi.org/10.1002/fld.537): momentum carried through the cells beside
  each face (Koren-limited u*) and through its corners, the local inertial flow depth of Bates et al. 2010
  (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.03.027) for the face velocity and dry faces, the mean depth over the face bed
  for the pressure (so a bore keeps its Rankine-Hugoniot speed), semi-implicit Manning friction n = 0.02 for sand
  (Chow 1959; at 5 cm a drag coefficient of 0.011, inside the swash values of Puleo and Holland 2001,
  https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-3839(01)00004-7) in place of the 0.12 /s decay, and the half-cell Courant cap. The
  outflow layout Water's surface, spray and queries read is unchanged. The surf's sea drive, which pulls the outflows
  of the open sea toward the swell's flux, moves water only across a wet face, as the momentum step does (without that
  mask it pushed the sea up over a 2 m bank into an enclosed pond, packages/water/test/flow.browser.mjs). The surf spins the flow up over its last 40 s
  before the first frame, in 1/45 s steps (`surf.ts` `SURF_SPIN`; Brocchini and Baldock 2008,
  https://doi.org/10.1029/2006RG000215), so the first frame shows the swash. Measured: the NOAA case runs up 0.0874
  (+1.5%), a dam-break bore runs 2.950 m/s against Stoker's 2.958 with the middle depth exact
  (packages/water/test/coast-runup.test.js); on the surf test's beach the swell runs 0.126 m up the sand in the first
  wave period and later, on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, against 0.155 m from Hunt's regular-wave law (1959) and 0.238 m
  significant run-up from Stockdon et al. 2006, and the old flow's 0.014 to 0.042 m (packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs,
  bound within 30% of Hunt). The run-up rises with finer cells (0.78 m cells here; docs/limits.md). The first frame
  costs about 0.4 s more on WebGPU (812 to 1,256 ms) and 3 s more on the WebGL2 layer (4.2 to 7.1 s) for the 512 x 82
  test grid. Regressions: packages/water/test/coast-runup.test.js, packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs,
  packages/water/test/rivers.test.js (the KB5736a fall on the new step).
- **Split out, fixed 2026-11-18:** `TerrainColors` darkened sand only where water stood at that moment, so a swash left
  no wet band behind it (KB-TERRAIN-WETSAND1).

### Fixed 2026-11-18: the sand dried the moment the swash left it (KB-TERRAIN-WETSAND1, terrain)

- **Repro:** a terrain-coupled `Water` with `TerrainColors` on sand: the sand was dark only under standing water, so
  the band a real beach shows behind the backwash (sand wet for minutes after each run-up) was missing.
  `node packages/terrain/test/wetness.browser.mjs` on the parent commit: one second after 10 cm of water leaves a
  flat beach its sRGB luma is back to 160.0 (dry) against 121.8 under water.
- **Cause:** `TerrainColors` read the coastal depth of the current frame only (its own comment: "use a persistent
  mask").
- **Fix:** terrain keeps a moisture record over the water's grid (`rgba32float`, one compute pass a frame): standing
  water fills moisture and surface film, which then fall as exp(-t / `wetDryTime`, default 900 s) and exp(-t /
  `wetGlossTime`, default 20 s); the darkening share is (1 - e^-3m) / (1 - e^-3) of the moisture, and the film sets the
  sheen (D. P. Horn 2002 and 2006, beach groundwater and the swash zone; R. A. Namikas et al. 2010, surface moisture of a
  fine-grained beach; D. B. Lobell and G. P. Asner 2002 and C. Nolet et al. 2014, reflectance against moisture;
  J. Lekner and M. Dorf 1988, S. A. Twomey et al. 1986, darkening). Measured on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer: one second
  after the water left 121.8 (as under water), 11 s on 123.3 against 123.3 for sand at the predicted darkening, one
  10 s dry time on 135.8 against 135.8, dried 160.0. Regressions: packages/terrain/test/wetness.browser.mjs,
  packages/terrain/test/colors.test.js.

### Fixed 2026-11-16: a sand beach got a flat grey sea and a white band at the waterline, no breaking surf (KB-WATER-SURF1, water)

- **Repro:** `node packages/scenes/test/dune-coast-still.mjs --views=surf,beach --w=1280 --h=720 --out=<folder>`
  on the parent commit: the sea is flat grey up to a bright white strip at the waterline, with no lines of breaking
  waves. `node packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs` fails there (the water shader has no surf).
- **Cause:** the open-sea forcing drove the shallow flow with the deep-water swell and faded it out between 2.4 and
  0.65 m of depth, so no wave shoaled, turned or broke; the flow's Froude breaker foam fired only in the last few
  centimetres, where it drew the white band (shore foam over every shallow cell added to it).
- **Fix:** a default surf in `@margoengine/water` (`src/surf.ts`): per-cell travel time from deep water (an eikonal
  relaxed on the GPU when the flow starts), Snell turning, depth wavenumber, linear shoaling, a 0.78 depth cap, a
  skewed breaking waveform, roller and trail foam, turbid broken water, and a hand-over to the flow at 0.9 to 0.35 m
  that drives its height and flux. Papers are cited in `src/surf.ts`. Regression: packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs
  (breaking in the surf zone, none and no foam deeper than 3 m, shoaling, the depth cap, the bores reaching dry sand).

### Fixed 2026-11-24: gltf/pbr's model nodes and the facade's meshes were two Mesh types, so parenting one to the other needed a cast (KB-GLTF-MESHTYPE1, gltf, core)

- **Repro:** `const model = await loadGLTF(engine, url); model.root.setParent(engine.createMesh());` failed to type-check
  (TS2740: the facade's `Mesh` lacks `engine`, `id`, `scene`, `born` and 4 more of the engine's internal `Mesh`).
- **Cause:** `PBRModel.root` and `nodes` were typed with `core/dist/engine`'s `Mesh`, `engine.createMesh` returns
  `core/dist/api`'s; at run time both are the same object.
- **Fix:** they are typed `ModelNode`, the engine's `Mesh` and the public `Mesh` at once, so `setParent` takes either
  and packages that read `model.root.engine` keep working; no core change. Regression: the gltf README example
  `model.root.setParent(turntable)` / `marker.setParent(model.nodes[0])`, type-checked by `npm run quality`
  (readme-types), fails with TS2740 on the old typing. `examples/kitty-hawk/main.ts` still carries its old cast.

### Fixed 2026-11-20: gltf/pbr's model nodes and the facade's meshes were two Mesh types, so parenting one to the other needed a cast (KB-GLTF-MESHTYPE1, gltf)

- **Repro:** `const model = await loadGLTF(engine, url); model.root.setParent(engine.createMesh());` failed to type-check
  (TS2740: the facade's `Mesh` lacks `engine`, `id`, `scene`, `born` and 4 more of the engine's internal `Mesh`).
- **Cause:** `PBRModel.root` and `nodes` were typed with `core/dist/engine`'s `Mesh`, whose `setParent` takes that
  internal type; `engine.createMesh` returns `core/dist/api`'s. At run time both are the same object.
- **Fix:** no core change and no change to a locked export: `PBRModel.root` and `nodes` in `@margoengine/gltf` are typed
  `Mesh & FacadeMesh` (the internal class and the public interface), so `setParent` accepts either. `examples/kitty-hawk`
  lost its cast. Regression: tests/public-engine-types.test.js (KB-GLTF-MESHTYPE1).

### Fixed 2026-11-27: particles blended over a surface did not veil its ambient light (KB-SSAO-BLENDVEIL1, post, vfx)

- **Repro (before):** `node packages/vfx/test/smoke-ao.browser.mjs`: 3,000 dark puffs (alpha 0.55) in front of the crease
  of a pale floor and wall under a strong ambient light, GTAO on: 1,143 of 76,800 pixels fell under their colour without
  GTAO times their visibility, worst by 0.186 in linear light (RTX A6000, WebGPU). Not seen in Fauld fr096, whose store
  has almost no ambient light underground.
- **Cause:** only `Scatter` registered an ambient veil (`packages/shared/ambient-veil.js`). The occlusion composite takes
  ambient * (1 - visibility) out of the pixel, and the replay held the wall's whole ambient light under puffs that left
  only 1 - alpha of the wall in the pixel, so it took more light than the pixel held.
- **Fix:** `packages/vfx/src/base.ts`: every `VFX` registers a veil that draws the same frame's billboards again over
  the replay target, black, blended `zero, one-minus-src-alpha`, so the light there keeps 1 - alpha of each puff
  (Porter and Duff's over, SIGGRAPH 1984; the revealage of McGuire and Bavoil, "Weighted Blended Order-Independent
  Transparency", JCGT 2013, https://jcgt.org/published/0002/02/09/). It draws only after the view's own billboard pass
  of the same frame and depth.
- **After:** 0 pixels under the bound (worst 0.021, inside the 0.04 tolerance), 3,357 pixels still occluded; the
  WebGL2 layer 0 and 3,585.
